e.t: Addi is a personal name, referring to an individual in the genealogy recorded in Luke. It is not presented as a descriptive word with a stated meaning, but as the name of one person in the line listed there. In the Greek New Testament, Addi occurs once, at Luke 3:28. The surrounding verse text is needed to say more about this person’s place in the genealogy, but the name itself identifies him rather than expressing an action, quality, or teaching.

This word means “of a goat” or “goat’s,” describing something that belongs to, comes from, or is associated with a goat. It is a specific descriptive term rather than a broad word for animals in general. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, at Hebrews 11:37. Without the verse text and surrounding context, its exact grammatical role there cannot be stated more precisely, but its basic meaning remains a goat-related description.

This word means “delay”—a postponement or holding back that causes something to happen later rather than immediately. In the Greek New Testament, it appears once, in Acts 25:17, and its ordinary sense is simply the idea of delaying or waiting before proceeding. The surrounding verse is needed to explain exactly how the delay functions in that passage, but the word itself points to an interval or postponement, not to the event being canceled or permanently refused.

This word means “remembrance” or “reminder”: something that brings a person, event, or truth back to mind. In the New Testament, it is used four times and especially describes a deliberate act of remembering, including the remembrance connected with Jesus’ supper and the repeated reminders provided by former sacrifices. Its central idea is not merely recalling information, but keeping something significant before the mind. The precise force in each passage comes from its surrounding context.

This word describes someone who is above reproach—without a legitimate accusation that brings blame or disgrace. It expresses a condition of being irreproachable, so that one's conduct cannot rightly be faulted. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs three times, all in 1 Timothy. Its uses concern the standard expected of believers and especially those serving faithfully, but the word itself states the character quality rather than detailing every circumstance. The surrounding passage determines how that blameless standing is being applied in each verse.

e.t: This Greek New Testament verb means “to leave,” “to go away from,” or simply “leaves.” It describes a person or group departing from someone or someplace rather than remaining there. The word occurs three times in the Greek New Testament, each in a different verse. Its exact force—whether a physical departure or separation from someone—depends on the surrounding sentence, but its central idea is moving away or leaving.

This word means “beginning” and can also refer to “rulers.” As a noun, it may point to the starting point or origin of something, or to people who hold governing authority. Its exact sense is determined by how it functions in the sentence. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs 55 times, showing use across a broad range of passages rather than referring to only one subject or setting.

e.t: This word means “to make secure” or “to secure”—to establish protection, stability, or dependable control over something. It is a verb describing an action rather than a person, object, or quality. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs four times: three times in Matthew and once in Acts. Its central idea remains the same wherever it appears: taking steps to prevent something from being disturbed, changed, escaped, or compromised. The precise force in any sentence depends on what is being secured and the surrounding passage.

This word means “chaff,” the light, useless material separated from useful grain after threshing. It refers to what is removed because it has no value as food and can be carried away or burned. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs twice, in Matthew 3:12 and Luke 3:17. Its ordinary meaning is therefore a concrete farming term, though its significance in either passage depends on the surrounding verse and comparison being made.

This Greek New Testament word means “life.” It can refer to life as a person’s living existence and, in some passages, to the means or resources that support that life. The word occurs 10 times in the Greek New Testament, including passages involving a widow’s offering, life amid worldly cares, and a person’s possessions. Its precise emphasis depends on the surrounding sentence, but its central idea remains life—what a person lives and, at times, what sustains that living.

This word refers to a difference or distinction between people, things, or categories. It draws attention to the fact that something is not the same as something else. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs three times, all in Romans and 1 Corinthians. Its meaning is straightforward, but the specific distinction being discussed must be understood from the surrounding verse and passage. The word appears in contexts where recognizing whether there is a difference matters to the point being made.

e.t: This word means “be separated” or “to be separated.” It describes people or things becoming distinct from one another rather than remaining together. As a Greek New Testament word, it appears once, in Luke 9:33. That single occurrence establishes its basic lexical sense, while the surrounding verse determines exactly what is being separated in that passage. The idea is straightforward: a division or parting takes place.

e.t: This word means “to distort” or “distorting,” describing the act of twisting something so that it no longer presents the matter truthfully. It functions as an action word, pointing to the alteration or misrepresentation of what is being communicated. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in 2 Corinthians 4:2. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central meaning concerns corrupting or falsifying a message rather than presenting it plainly.

e.t: This Greek New Testament word means “to get into.” It describes entering or boarding something, functioning as an action word rather than naming a person, place, or object. It occurs 16 times across 16 New Testament verses, including passages involving people getting into a boat or onto a vessel. The basic idea is movement into or aboard something. The exact force in a particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence, but its normal meaning remains straightforward: to enter, get inside, or board.

e.t: This Greek verb means “to make a sign” or “to signify.” It describes communicating meaning through a sign or gesture rather than through spoken words. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, so its normal meaning is clear even though its particular force depends on the surrounding verse and passage. The word therefore points to an intentional act of signaling—using a visible indication to communicate something to another person.

e.t: This word means “immediately”: something happens at once, without waiting or a noticeable delay. It is an adverb, so it describes how quickly an action or response occurs rather than naming a person, place, or thing. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs six times, including several occurrences in Acts and one each in Mark and Philippians. Its repeated rendering as “immediately” supports the consistent sense of prompt action across these passages.

This word describes someone or something that is leading or prominent—standing out because of a superior or noticeable position. It points to distinction or prominence rather than merely being present. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Acts 25:23, so its precise force in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and context. Its central idea remains clear: what is prominent, distinguished, or occupying a leading place.

This word describes knowing or understanding, pointing to someone who possesses insight or comprehension. It presents understanding as a quality a person may have, rather than as an action or command. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in James 3:13. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central meaning remains clear: a person who knows and understands. The English rendering “understanding” reflects this sense.

“Heavenly” describes something as belonging to or associated with heaven. This Greek New Testament adjective identifies a heavenly reality, distinguishing it from what is earthly, while the surrounding sentence determines its specific reference. The word occurs 19 times in the Greek New Testament, including passages in John, 1 Corinthians, Ephesians, and Hebrews. Its precise force—whether describing a place, sphere, or quality—depends on the context where it appears.

e.t: This New Testament word means “to have a chance to” or “to have opportunity.” It describes having an available occasion or suitable opening to do something. The word occurs three times in the Greek New Testament, each in a different verse, so it expresses a specific idea rather than a broad range of unrelated meanings. Its exact force in any verse depends on what action or circumstance surrounds the opportunity, but the central sense remains the availability of a chance to act.

e.t: This word means “approached” or “to approach,” describing someone or something coming near. It can refer to a person drawing close, a group arriving, or an event coming upon people. The word appears 21 times in the Greek New Testament, so its basic sense is used in more than one kind of situation. The exact force—whether a person arrives, comes forward, or something draws near—depends on the sentence and surrounding passage.

This word describes something peaceful and quiet—calm rather than noisy, troubled, or disruptive. It presents quietness as a settled condition, emphasizing peaceful conduct or surroundings rather than agitation. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in 1 Timothy 2:2. Its precise force in that verse belongs to the surrounding passage, but the word itself points to a calm, undisturbed quality. “Peaceful” and “quiet” capture its central meaning.

This word means “appearance”—the way someone or something is visibly presented or seen. It describes what is observable in outward form, rather than necessarily explaining the person’s identity or inner nature. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Matthew 28:3. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central sense remains the visible appearance or presentation of something.

e.t: This word means “to be numbered among” or “to number.” It describes counting someone as part of a group, or the act of assigning people or things a place in a numbered group. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Acts 1:17. Its wording emphasizes inclusion within an identified group rather than merely noticing or listing someone. The surrounding verse supplies the specific situation in which this idea is expressed.

me: Verb, Aorist, Active, Indicative, third, Singular

e.t: This word means “to pour” or “to pour out.” It describes the action of causing a liquid or other substance to flow from one place or container into another. As a verb, it focuses on the act of pouring rather than on the substance itself. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs twice, once in Matthew and once in Mark. Its precise force in either verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning remains the deliberate pouring out of something.

gl: basket of various sizes and considered typical of the Jews

e.t: This word means “basket,” referring to a container used to hold or carry things. Its fuller sense can include a basket of various sizes, described as typical of the Jews. In the Greek New Testament, it appears six times, each time rendered “baskets.” The word occurs in accounts where baskets are associated with gathering or carrying what remained after people had eaten, though the exact force in any particular verse depends on its surrounding passage.

This Greek New Testament word means “captain” or “sea captain,” referring to the person who serves as captain at sea. It is a specific noun for a maritime leader, rather than a general title for every kind of commander. The word occurs twice in the Greek New Testament, in Acts and Revelation, showing the term in two separate passages without changing its basic meaning. Its precise role in either verse depends on the surrounding context.

This word means “made of stone” or refers to “stone.” It describes a material or object connected with stone, presenting stone as the central physical idea. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs three times, appearing once each in John, 2 Corinthians, and Revelation. Its ordinary meaning remains focused on stone rather than on a symbolic idea by itself; the surrounding verse determines how that stone-related description functions in context.

This Greek New Testament word means “bridegroom,” referring to the man associated with a wedding as the groom. It is a specific title for the male participant in marriage celebrations, rather than a general word for any guest or family member. The word occurs three times in the Greek New Testament, appearing once each in Matthew, Mark, and Luke. Its precise significance in any one passage depends on the surrounding verse and discussion. The word means “eye,” referring to the organ of sight. It is used as a physical noun for the eyes of a person, rather than as an abstract idea. In the Greek New Testament, this word occurs twice, in Matthew 20:34 and Mark 8:23. Its ordinary sense is the bodily organ through which a person sees. The precise force in either passage depends on the surrounding verse and passage.

me: ADVerb or adverb and particle combined

e.t: This Greek New Testament word means “no longer” or “not any more.” It is used to mark that something has stopped being true, happening, or continuing, distinguishing a former condition from the present one. Thus, it points to a change over time rather than simply expressing a general denial. The word occurs 47 times in the Greek New Testament, showing repeated use for situations in which a prior state has ended or will not continue.

This word means a lawbreaker or transgressor—someone who crosses a stated boundary or violates a law. It describes a person in relation to a command that has been broken, rather than merely someone who makes an accidental mistake. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs five times, in Romans, Galatians, and James. Its precise force in any one verse depends on the command or standard being discussed there.

me: Noun, Nominative, Plural, Masculine, Location Gentilic

e.t: This word refers to a Parthian—someone identified as belonging to the Parthians, a people or group named in the New Testament. It is a proper ethnic designation rather than a description of an action, quality, or belief. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Acts 2:9. The word’s precise role there is best understood from the surrounding verse and passage.

This word describes a person who is living among people of another place or community as a foreigner or stranger. It can refer to someone viewed as an outsider because they do not belong to the surrounding society. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs four times, including language about foreigners and those regarded as strange. Its exact emphasis—whether residence, social belonging, or unfamiliarity—depends on the sentence and surrounding passage.

This word refers to “refuse” or “scum”—something regarded as worthless and fit to be cast away. It describes what people reject rather than value. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in 1 Corinthians 4:13. Its basic sense is clear from these meanings, while the surrounding verse is needed to show exactly how the word functions there. It should be understood as a strong term for unwanted waste or something treated as contemptible.

me: Verb, Aorist, Middle, Participle, Genitive, Singular, Masculine

e.t: This Greek New Testament word means “to foresee,” and can also express “to plan.” It describes looking ahead to what is intended or arranged, rather than merely reacting to what has already happened. As a verb, it presents foresight or prior purpose in an action. It occurs once in the Greek New Testament, in Hebrews 11:40, so its precise force there depends on the surrounding verse and passage.

me: Verb, Present, Active, Indicative, second, Singular

e.t: This word means “to owe” or “to owe besides.” It describes being under an obligation to give or repay something, with the added sense of owing something in addition to what has already been mentioned. It is a verb, so it expresses the action or condition of owing rather than naming the debt itself. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Philemon 1:19. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding wording, but its central idea is an additional obligation or debt.

This word means “tossing” or “tossing motion,” describing movement that is unsettled, shaken, or thrown about. It presents the idea of motion rather than a person, object, or settled condition. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Luke 21:25. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central meaning remains the image of tossing movement. This word therefore helps readers picture instability or agitation expressed through motion, without by itself specifying what causes that movement or how long it continues.

This word describes a sharer—someone who has a part in something together with others. It points to participation or partnership rather than merely observing from the outside. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs four times, including passages concerning shared spiritual benefit, shared service, shared suffering, and shared fellowship. The exact aspect of participation depends on the surrounding sentence, but the central idea remains one of joining with others in what they experience, receive, or do.

This word refers to a sycamore tree, also described as a sycamore-fig tree. It is the name of a particular kind of tree rather than a description of a person, action, or spiritual quality. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Luke 19:4. The precise significance of the tree in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but the word itself identifies the tree that is mentioned there.

me: Verb, Present, Active, Participle, Genitive, Singular, Masculine

e.t: This word means “to come together” or “to gather.” It describes people moving into a shared gathering rather than remaining separate. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Luke 8:4. Its basic sense focuses on the act of coming together, while the surrounding passage determines who gathers and why. The word therefore presents gathering as a shared movement or assembly, without by itself specifying the purpose, size, or result of that gathering.

e.t: This word means “I delight” or “to delight in agreement.” It expresses an active enjoyment or inner pleasure that comes from sharing the same view or desire. As a verb, it describes what someone does rather than naming a person, object, or quality. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Romans 7:22. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central idea is taking genuine pleasure in agreement with something or someone.

me: Verb, Present, Passive, Participle, Accusative, Singular, Neuter

e.t: This word describes something running over or overflowing, so that it goes beyond its normal limit. It presents an image of abundance spilling out rather than remaining contained. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Luke 6:38. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding words and passage, but its central meaning is the action of overflowing or being poured out beyond measure.

This Greek New Testament word means “snow.” It refers to the white, frozen precipitation that falls from the sky. The word occurs twice in the Greek New Testament, in Matthew and Revelation, and its ordinary meaning remains the same in both places. Understanding this basic sense helps readers recognize when Scripture uses snow as a visible description, without assigning a more specific meaning apart from the surrounding verse and passage.
